topics.title: Relevant Definitions under GST
explain: Goods [Sec 2(52)] means every kind of movable property other than money and securities, but includes actionable claims, growing crops, grass, and things attached to land agreed to be severed.
Services [Sec 2(102)] means anything other than goods, money, and securities, but includes activities relating to the use of money or its conversion for separate consideration.
Consideration [Sec 2(31)] includes payment in money or kind and monetary value of any act or forbearance, excluding Central or State Government subsidies.
Refundable security deposits are not consideration unless applied by the supplier against the supply.
Person [Sec 2(84)] includes individuals, HUF, companies, firms, LLPs, local authorities, Government, trusts, and artificial juridical persons.
Taxable Territory [Sec 2(109)] is the territory where CGST Act applies; India [Sec 2(56)] includes territorial waters, seabed, EEZ, and airspace.

flow.title: Classification under GST Definitions
steps: Identify item being transferred
Is it money or securities?
If yes, excluded from goods & services
Is it movable property or crop/claim?
If yes, classified as Goods
Else anything else is classified as Services

topics.example: A bank charges a service fee for converting US Dollars to Indian Rupees. The currency is money, but the conversion activity for a separate fee is a taxable Service under Section 2(102).
remember: Money and securities are neither goods nor services under GST.
Actionable claims, growing crops, and grass are specifically included in the definition of goods.
mistakes: Treating securities as goods. Securities are explicitly excluded from both goods and services.

quiz.q: Which of the following is specifically included in the definition of 'Goods' under Section 2(52)?
quiz.why: Actionable claims, growing crops, and grass are specifically included under goods, while money and securities are excluded.

quiz.q: How is a refundable deposit treated for GST consideration purposes under Section 2(31)?
o: Never treated as consideration under any circumstance
Not treated as payment unless applied by the supplier to the supply
Taxed at a flat rate of 18% automatically
quiz.why: A deposit is not considered payment unless the supplier applies such deposit as consideration for the supply.

topics.title: Meaning and Scope of Supply & Parameters
explain: Section 7(1)(a) gives an inclusive definition of supply covering sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease, or disposal.
Three parameters must be satisfied: (1) Supply of goods or services, (2) Made for consideration, (3) In course or furtherance of business.
Business [Sec 2(17)] includes trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, race club operations, RWA services, or admission to premises.
Frequency, volume, continuity, or profit motive are not prerequisites for an activity to qualify as business.
Donations received by charitable/religious entities without commercial publicity or quid pro quo are outside the scope of supply.

flow.title: Testing a Transaction under Section 7(1)(a)
steps: Is it goods, services, or both?
Is there a valid form of supply?
Is consideration present in money/kind?
Is it in course or furtherance of business?
If all yes, it is a Supply

topics.example: Rishabh sells his personal car to a second-hand dealer after using it for a year. Since the sale is not in the course of Rishabh's business, it is not a supply under GST.
remember: Supply must meet all three parameters under Section 7(1)(a): Goods/Services + Consideration + Business course.
Personal sales by individuals are outside the course or furtherance of business.
mistakes: Assuming profit motive or regular transaction frequency is needed for an activity to be called business.

quiz.q: A doctor gets a haircut from a barber and provides medical advice to the barber in return without cash changing hands. What is this transaction?
o: Barter transaction constituting supply for both
quiz.why: Barter of services where each party provides a service as consideration for another is a supply by both parties.

quiz.q: A donor donates money to a hospital, and the hospital places a plaque stating 'Donated by Mr. X'. Is GST applicable on this donation?
o: Yes, taxed at 18% as commercial sponsorship
No, because there is no quid pro quo or commercial publicity
No, only if the donor is a registered business
quiz.why: Expression of gratitude without commercial advertising or business promotion lacks quid pro quo and is not a supply.

topics.title: Importation of Services for Consideration
explain: Importation of services for a consideration is treated as a supply under Section 7(1)(b).
Crucial rule: It qualifies as a supply whether or not it is in the course or furtherance of business.
This is the only exception where the business furtherance test is relaxed for supplies made with consideration.
Importing overseas services for personal use (e.g., personal residence design) attracts GST if paid for.

flow.title: Import of Service with Consideration Rule
steps: Service received from outside India
Consideration paid to overseas supplier
Is it for business or personal use?
Business relevance is not required
Qualifies as Supply under Section 7(1)(b)

topics.example: Ramaiyaa hires an architect from New York for $5,000 to design his personal residential house in Delhi. This is a supply under Section 7(1)(b) even though it is for personal use.
remember: Import of service + Consideration = Always a Supply under Section 7(1)(b).
mistakes: Believing personal imports of services with consideration are outside GST. Section 7(1)(b) explicitly includes personal imports for consideration.

quiz.q: An individual imports legal consultancy services from a UK firm for personal family disputes and pays US$ 1,000. Does this qualify as a supply under GST?
o: No, because it is for personal use
Yes, under Section 7(1)(b) as consideration is present
No, because no Indian tax invoice was raised
Yes, but only if the individual has a GST registration
quiz.why: Import of service for consideration is a supply under Section 7(1)(b) whether or not in course or furtherance of business.

quiz.q: Which parameter of supply is relaxed specifically under Section 7(1)(b) for imported services?
o: Requirement of being in course or furtherance of business
quiz.why: Section 7(1)(b) explicitly states that import of services for consideration is a supply whether or not in course or furtherance of business.

topics.title: Deemed Supply: Activities Without Consideration
explain: Section 7(1)(c) treats specified activities as supply even if made WITHOUT consideration (Deemed Supply).
Para 1: Permanent transfer/disposal of business assets where Input Tax Credit (ITC) has been availed.

Para 2: Supply of goods/services between related persons or distinct persons [Sec 25] in the course/furtherance of business. Employer gifts to employees up to Rs. 50,000 per financial year are NOT supply. Contractual perquisites are also outside GST.

Para 3: Supply of goods between Principal and Agent where the agent issues/receives invoices in their own name. Del-credere agent (DCA) issuing invoice in own name subsumes credit extension into main supply.
Para 4: Import of services by a person from a related person or establishment outside India in the course or furtherance of business without consideration.

flow.title: Schedule I Deemed Supply Evaluation
steps: Is consideration absent?
Permanent asset transfer with ITC availed? -> Supply
Transaction between related/distinct persons for business? -> Supply
Principal-Agent invoice in agent name? -> Supply
Import of service from related entity for business? -> Supply
If none apply -> Not a Supply

topics.example: Dhruv gifts old business laptops to a friend for free. Since Dhruv claimed ITC on these laptops, it is a deemed supply under Para 1 of Schedule I.
remember: Employer gifts to an employee up to Rs. 50,000 in a financial year are not treated as supply.
Principal-Agent rule under Schedule I Para 3 applies ONLY to goods, not services.
mistakes: Treating branch transfers within the same state under a single GST registration as supply. Only distinct persons (separate registrations) trigger deemed supply.

quiz.q: A company gifts laptops worth Rs. 60,000 to an employee during Diwali. What is the GST treatment under Schedule I?
o: Exempt as an employee welfare expense
Fully treated as supply since gift value exceeds Rs. 50,000
Taxable only on the excess Rs. 10,000
Not a supply under any circumstances
quiz.why: Gifts exceeding Rs. 50,000 in a financial year by an employer to an employee qualify as supply under Schedule I Para 2.

quiz.q: An agent procures goods for a principal. The invoice from the supplier is issued directly in the principal's name. Does the agent fall under Para 3 of Schedule I?
o: Yes, all agents fall under Schedule I
No, because the invoice is in the name of the principal
Yes, if the agent receives commission
No, unless the transaction exceeds Rs. 2,50,000
quiz.why: Schedule I Para 3 applies only when the agent has authority to issue or receive invoices in their own name.

topics.title: Transactions between Non-Individual Person and Members
explain: Section 7(1)(aa) covers transactions between a person (other than an individual) and its members/constituents for valuable consideration.
Examples include Resident Welfare Associations (RWAs), clubs, and trade associations supplying goods or services to members.
The explanation clarifies that the person and its members are deemed to be two separate persons.
This provision overrules the common law 'doctrine of mutuality' with retrospective effect.

flow.title: Testing Member-Association Transactions
steps: Is the supplier an association/club/RWA?
Is the transaction with its own members?
Is consideration involved?
Deem entity and member as separate persons
Qualifies as Supply under Section 7(1)(aa)

topics.example: A Resident Welfare Association (RWA) collects monthly maintenance fees from its members to provide security and facility management. This is a supply under Section 7(1)(aa).
remember: Section 7(1)(aa) applies with overriding effect over any other law or court judgment to negate the doctrine of mutuality.
mistakes: Assuming club services to members are non-taxable due to mutuality of interest.

quiz.q: A sports club provides gym facilities to its members for a monthly fee. How is this treated under GST?
o: Outside GST due to doctrine of mutuality
quiz.why: Section 7(1)(aa) explicitly states that transactions between a non-individual person and its members for consideration constitute a supply.

quiz.q: What legal doctrine was overridden by the introduction of Section 7(1)(aa)?
quiz.why: Section 7(1)(aa) overrules the doctrine of mutuality, treating an association and its members as distinct legal entities for GST.

topics.title: Classification of Supply: Goods vs Services
explain: Once an activity is a supply, Section 7(1A) read with Schedule II classifies whether it is a supply of GOODS or SERVICES.
Transfer of title in goods = Goods; Right/undivided share without title transfer = Services; Hire purchase / Future title transfer = Goods.
Leasing/renting of land or building = Services. Transfer of tenancy rights (Pagadi premium) = Services.
Job work (treatment or process on another person's goods) = Services.
Permanent transfer of business assets = Goods; Business assets put to private use = Services; Goods left upon winding up business = Goods.
Construction of complex/building before Completion Certificate (CC) or first occupation = Services. Renting of immovable property = Services.
Temporary IP transfer, IT software development, agreeing to refrain/tolerate/do an act, right to use goods = Services.
Works contract [Sec 2(119)] and Restaurant/catering services are composite supplies deemed as Supply of Services.

flow.title: Schedule II Classification Decision Tree
steps: Is title in goods transferred permanently? -> Goods
Is right to use transferred without title? -> Services
Is it job work or process on others' goods? -> Services
Is it leasing/renting/construction before CC? -> Services
Is it works contract or restaurant service? -> Services

topics.example: Genius Equipments Ltd. gives machinery on rent to Suhaasi Manufacturers without transferring ownership. Under Schedule II Para 1(b), this is a Supply of Services.
remember: Works contract and restaurant services are specifically classified as Supply of Services under Schedule II.
mistakes: Classifying job work as supply of goods. Job work is a process on another person's goods and is always a Supply of Services.

quiz.q: Damani Dyeing House dyes raw fabrics belonging to Shubham Textiles on a job work basis. How is this classified under Schedule II?
o: Neither Supply of Goods nor Services
quiz.why: Schedule II Para 3 states that any treatment or process applied to another person's goods is a Supply of Services.

quiz.q: A manufacturer supplies goods on a hire-purchase agreement where ownership passes after all installments are paid. How is this classified under Schedule II?
quiz.why: Schedule II Para 1(c) classifies any transfer of title under an agreement where property passes at a future date upon payment of full consideration as a Supply of Goods.

topics.title: Non-Supplies under GST (Negative List)
explain: Section 7(2)(a) read with Schedule III lists activities treated NEITHER as supply of goods nor supply of services (Negative List).

Schedule III entries: (1) Employee services to employer in employment course, (2) Court/Tribunal services, (3) Functions of MPs, MLAs, Constitutional post holders, (4) Mortuary/funeral services including transport of deceased, (5) Sale of land & completed building (after CC/first occupation), (6) Actionable claims OTHER THAN specified 6, (9 & 10) Co-insurance premium apportionment & reinsurance ceding commission.
Specified actionable claims ARE taxable supplies: betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery, and online money gaming.
Section 7(2)(b) Notified Non-Supplies: Panchayat functions (Art 243G), Municipality functions (Art 243W), and Grant of alcoholic liquor license by State Governments.
Inter-state movement of conveyances (trucks, buses, trains, cranes) for carrying goods/passengers or repairs (not for further supply) is treated as non-supply.

flow.title: Checking Non-Supply Status
steps: Is it employee service in course of employment? -> Non-Supply
Is it court, MP/MLA function, or funeral service? -> Non-Supply
Is it sale of land or completed building after CC? -> Non-Supply
Is it actionable claim other than specified 6? -> Non-Supply
Is it liquor licence grant or Panchayat function? -> Non-Supply
If matched -> Outside GST scope

topics.example: ABC Ltd. sells a commercial building to a buyer after receiving the Completion Certificate from local authorities. This falls under Schedule III Para 5 and is not a supply under GST.
remember: Specified actionable claims (lottery, betting, gambling, horse racing, casinos, online money gaming) are taxable supplies.
Grant of alcoholic liquor licence by State Governments is a notified non-supply.
mistakes: Thinking state government grant of alcoholic liquor licence attracts GST under reverse charge.

quiz.q: Which of the following actionable claims is treated as a taxable supply under GST?
quiz.why: Specified actionable claims (including online money gaming, lottery, betting, etc.) are excluded from Schedule III and treated as supplies.

quiz.q: Inter-state movement of trucks between distinct branches of a logistics firm for carrying out repair and maintenance is treated as:
o: Neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services
Supply of repair services subject to IGST on truck value
quiz.why: Circular clarifications state inter-state movement of conveyances for repairs/maintenance (not for further supply) is treated as neither a supply of goods nor services.

topics.title: Composite and Mixed Supplies
explain: Section 8 outlines tax liability when two or more items or services are supplied together.
Composite Supply [Sec 2(30)]: Two or more taxable supplies naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction in ordinary course of business, where one is a principal supply [Sec 2(90)].
Tax liability of Composite Supply: Treated as supply of the PRINCIPAL SUPPLY and taxed at the principal supply's GST rate [Sec 8(a)].
Mixed Supply [Sec 2(74)]: Two or more individual supplies made together for a single price, NOT naturally bundled.
Tax liability of Mixed Supply: Treated as supply of that item which attracts the HIGHEST RATE OF TAX [Sec 8(b)].
Printing books/annual reports (publisher gives content) = Supply of Services (printing is principal). Printing custom boxes/envelopes = Supply of Goods (box/paper is principal).

flow.title: Composite vs Mixed Supply Tax Treatment
steps: Are multiple items supplied together?
Is a single price charged or naturally bundled?
Are items naturally bundled in business course?
If Yes -> Composite Supply -> Tax at Principal Supply Rate
If No & single price -> Mixed Supply -> Tax at Highest Rate

topics.example: Rati Computers sells a laptop (18% GST) bundled with a laptop bag (28% GST) for a total price of Rs. 55,000. Being naturally bundled, it is a Composite Supply taxed at 18% (laptop rate).
remember: Composite supply = Naturally bundled = Taxed at Principal Supply rate.
Mixed supply = Not naturally bundled + Single price = Taxed at Highest rate.
mistakes: Assuming a gift pack containing chocolates (18%), juice (5%), and toys (5%) sold for a single price is a composite supply. It is a Mixed Supply taxed at 18%.

quiz.q: A dealer supplies a package containing canned foods, chocolates, and aerated drinks for a single lump-sum price of Rs. 1,000. How is this supply taxed under Section 8?
o: As a composite supply at the rate of canned foods
Taxed at individual rates for each item
As a mixed supply at the highest GST rate among the items
quiz.why: Items not naturally bundled supplied for a single price form a Mixed Supply, attracting the highest GST rate among the bundled items.

quiz.q: A publisher supplies content to a printer who supplies paper and prints 1,000 copies of a book. What is the classification of this supply by the printer?
quiz.why: In printing books/brochures where content is supplied by the publisher, printing is the principal supply, making it a Supply of Services.
